title: Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm

concept.text: The innovation is an actual quantum execution of Shor’s algorithm that solves a cryptographic instance at a deployed key size: for example, factoring a 2048-bit RSA modulus or recovering a discrete logarithm for a public key on a deployed 256-bit elliptic curve. Shor’s algorithm already supplies the mathematical method. The missing advance is a quantum computer capable of completing the required computation reliably, with independently checkable answers and evidence that the quantum device produced them.

This is an execution milestone. A resource estimate describes a possible machine; a small compiled experiment demonstrates selected algorithmic operations; a cryptographically relevant execution must carry the computation through at the target scale. The supplied studies describe routes toward that capability and useful component demonstrations, but do not demonstrate its achievement.

significance.text: Successful execution would turn a theoretical quantum threat into an experimentally demonstrated ability to recover secrets underlying widely deployed public-key cryptography. For an RSA instance the machine can factor, the factors undermine the corresponding RSA security. For an elliptic-curve public key whose discrete logarithm it can recover, the result exposes the associated private key. The revolutionary consequence is a concrete break of security resting on those mathematical problems and parameters.

The consequences would depend on the protocol and the information available to an attacker. Recorded traffic could become decryptable where captured protocol data and recovered secrets suffice; this does not imply that every recorded internet session becomes readable. Cryptocurrency exposure would likewise depend on the scheme and public-key exposure. The cat-qubit compilation paper identifies exposed public keys, including certain Bitcoin outputs and reused addresses, as relevant attack targets rather than establishing a threat to every asset.

One successful RSA factorization would not itself demonstrate an elliptic-curve attack, and success on one curve would not establish practical attacks on every deployed curve. Additional targets require suitable circuits, resources and runtimes. A universal machine’s existence alone is insufficient: its usable scale and reliability must support the relevant computation. Migration to quantum-resistant cryptography is a response to this threat, while the milestone itself is the verified factorization or discrete logarithm accompanied by evidence of quantum execution.

Conceptual synthesis: an expensive, slow or specialized implementation could still establish this breakthrough. Its operating cost and throughput would determine how broadly the capability could be used. Success would neither automatically deliver other quantum applications nor prove that factoring is classically hard; those are separate scientific questions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is sustained, fault-tolerant execution of a cryptographically sized factoring or discrete-logarithm circuit. This requires enough protected computational capacity, sufficiently reliable operations, and coordinated error correction and classical control to complete the entire calculation. Qubit count alone does not establish feasibility: the estimates also depend on connectivity, error models, correction-cycle speed and the time needed to react to measurement outcomes.

For the surface-code route, the engineering challenge includes realizing the assumed square nearest-neighbor architecture with uniform 0.1% depolarizing gate noise, 1 μs correction cycles and 10 μs reaction time at the required scale. Gidney’s estimate also contains algorithmic and architectural assumptions, and leaves further analysis of cold storage to future work. These assumptions define a conditional route to the target, rather than a complete experimental validation of every subsystem.

For the cat-qubit route, suppressing one error channel does not eliminate the need to control the other. The most compact supplied estimate assumes negligible bit flips, interpreted as a bit-flip time of about 100 years, while also assuming a phase-flip probability of 5 × 10⁻⁴ per 1 μs correction cycle. Allowing a bit-flip time of about one hour requires an additional protection layer and roughly doubles the estimated qubit count. A controlled single cat qubit with long bit-flip lifetime does not establish that thousands of interacting qubits can maintain the full set of assumed properties throughout a multiday computation.

Engineering synthesis: the central integration barrier is preserving the required performance while combining qubits, gates, measurements, error correction and classical processing into one operating machine. Comparing architectures therefore requires their complete noise and timing assumptions, rather than comparing headline qubit counts or isolated memory lifetimes.

current_state.text: Enrique Martín-López and collaborators’ 2012 Nature Photonics experiment demonstrated a compiled two-photon implementation that factored N = 21 using qubit recycling. Its circuit was constructed for the particular case N = 21 and x = 4, using known structure and explicitly calculated evolution. It demonstrated meaningful quantum interference and scalable recycling ideas, but was not a cryptographic-scale factorization. This historical result does not establish the worldwide experimental frontier in 2026.

Craig Gidney’s arXiv work submitted on 21 May 2025 estimates that a 2048-bit RSA integer could be factored in less than a week using fewer than one million noisy qubits. The stated physical assumptions include a square nearest-neighbor grid, uniform 0.1% depolarizing gate noise, a 1 μs surface-code cycle and a 10 μs reaction time. This is a conditional resource estimate, not a hardware execution. The supplied review had the complete 40-page paper available; it also identified additional algorithmic assumptions and deferred cold-storage analysis.

The cat-qubit compilation preprint by Axel Pappalardo, Dahmun Goudarzi and collaborators, dated 27 October 2026, estimates RSA-2048 factoring with 22,593 cat qubits—approximately 23,000—in 3.14 days. That configuration assumes 1 μs error-correction cycles, 10 μs reaction time, phase-flip probability pZ = 5 × 10⁻⁴ and negligible bit flips, corresponding to a bit-flip time of about 100 years. With a bit-flip time of about one hour, an additional protection layer raises the estimate to approximately 45,000 cat qubits and a runtime of at least 3.14 days. These figures describe projected configurations under different error assumptions.

The retained extraction of that 128-page cat-qubit paper ends on page 30. Its visible sections support the quoted estimates and benchmark discussion, but the detailed derivation in Appendix C9 and the experimental-state appendix were outside the available extraction. Consequently, the supplied material permits reporting those estimates but does not support treating the entire derivation or its survey of hardware progress as fully examined.

U. Réglade and collaborators’ 2024 Nature paper reports control of a single cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds. The associated author responses report phase-flip times ranging from 2.7 μs at cat size |α|² = 2.5 to 490 ns at |α|² = 11.3. These are measurements at different cat sizes, so they should not be combined into one simultaneous operating point. They also rule out the blanket characterization that phase-flip times were all below one microsecond. The main article was available as a subscription preview; the phase-flip range comes from the associated peer-review file.

The reported single-qubit experiment does not demonstrate the hour-scale or century-scale bit-flip times assumed in the two cited factoring configurations, nor does it demonstrate a complete factoring machine. The supplied evidence contains no cryptographically relevant execution. It also contains no comprehensive freshness survey establishing worldwide nonachievement as of 1 November 2026. The retained arXiv versions establish preprint provenance, but do not establish the absence of later journal publication. Those limits leave current global status open; they do not invalidate the dated experiments or resource estimates.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: execute quantum factoring of an independently selected standard 2048-bit RSA modulus whose factors are initially unknown to the demonstrators, or recover the discrete logarithm of an independently selected public key on a deployed 256-bit elliptic curve whose private key is initially unknown to them. These are proposed milestones grounded in the supplied cryptographic benchmarks, not established consensus standards. Either would establish the corresponding capability at that target size.
completion_criteria.label: Quantum-solve unknown 2048-bit RSA or unknown 256-bit elliptic discrete log

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence package: publish the factors or recovered discrete logarithm, the circuit and compilation method, device description, runtime, measurement records and classical processing needed to assess the execution. Multiplication can verify a factorization, and the corresponding public-key calculation can verify a recovered discrete logarithm. Correctness of the answer and evidence of its quantum provenance are separate requirements; a correct answer alone does not establish that a quantum device computed it.
completion_criteria.label: Published verifiable factors or discrete log with quantum provenance records

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: repeat the demonstration on additional independently selected instances and make the procedure sufficiently explicit for independent assessment and, where feasible, replication. Report success rates, failed attempts, total runtime, physical resources and classical processing costs. Such finite tests establish demonstrated breadth and operating reliability; they do not establish literal universality across all moduli, curves or implementations. Commercially attractive cost or throughput would be a further practical achievement, rather than a prerequisite for the first convincing execution.
completion_criteria.label: Assessable repeats on independent instances with reliability and resource costs

completion_criteria.text: A compiled circuit for a preselected tiny integer would not satisfy this proposal. The N = 21 experiment illustrates why: a circuit built around a known small instance can demonstrate valuable quantum operations without establishing the ability to solve an independently chosen cryptographic problem. The relevant distinction is the demonstrated computational scope and treatment of prior knowledge.
completion_criteria.label: Independently chosen cryptographic problem solved without prior knowledge

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: QUA-01, “Distance-scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computation,” concerns a general ability to preserve and process quantum information as protection increases. QUA-02 concerns completing one demanding cryptographic application. General fault-tolerant capability is closely relevant to its implementation, but demonstrating that capability alone does not establish completion of the required cryptographic circuit.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-04, “A laboratory material that stores a logical qubit passively at nonzero temperature,” and QUA-05, “Universal computation by braiding non-Abelian anyons,” concern distinct physical approaches to quantum protection or computation. Either could be relevant to a future implementation, but passive storage or braiding-based universality would not itself demonstrate cryptographic execution. QUA-06, “Fault-tolerant quantum interconnects that let processors scale by adding modules,” addresses a possible scaling mechanism rather than the cryptographic result.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-08, “Local, universal fault tolerance whose overhead stays bounded as the error falls,” addresses the cost of obtaining reliable computation. QUA-02 could be achieved with high overhead, while lower overhead could make later executions more practical. The supplied title supports this distinction, but does not establish QUA-08’s detailed technical requirements or whether it would precede or follow QUA-02. QUA-10, “Foundry-made fault-tolerant quantum computation without a dilution refrigerator,” similarly specifies a manufacturing and operating platform that QUA-02 does not require.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-07, “A proof that quantum polynomial time exceeds classical polynomial time on decision problems,” is a complexity-theoretic separation. Executing Shor’s algorithm at a deployed key size would not prove that separation or prove classical factoring hardness. Conversely, a complexity separation would not by itself supply a working cryptographic attack.

Roster-based synthesis: QUA-03, “Experimentally confirmed quantum prediction of sign-problematic matter,” and QUA-09, “An end-to-end superpolynomial quantum speedup on large classical data,” concern different application outcomes and evidence requirements. They overlap with QUA-02 in requiring more than an abstract algorithm or isolated component demonstration, but a successful cryptographic execution would not establish either material prediction or an end-to-end speedup on large classical data.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim that a modest universal machine would leave recorded traffic unreadable with a conditional explanation of secret recovery and possible decryption.
change_log.reason: The original opening obscured the intended cryptographic consequence and did not specify sufficient computational resources.

change_log.change: Separated RSA factorization, elliptic-curve discrete-log recovery, recorded-traffic exposure and cryptocurrency consequences.
change_log.reason: One demonstrated attack does not establish all others; consequences depend on parameters, protocols, captured data and public-key exposure.

change_log.change: Retained the 2025 resource estimate and added its connectivity, noise, timing and analysis qualifications.
change_log.reason: The numerical result is supported as a conditional estimate, while its assumptions materially affect feasibility.

change_log.change: Preserved and refined the October 2026 cat-qubit estimates, including 22,593 qubits, 3.14 days, error assumptions and the approximately 45,000-qubit alternative.
change_log.reason: The visible material supports these projections, but their differing protection assumptions prevent a simple headline comparison.

change_log.change: Replaced the blanket sub-microsecond phase-flip claim with the reported 2.7 μs to 490 ns range at different cat sizes.
change_log.reason: The associated author responses contradict the original characterization, and the abstract’s lower bound does not establish an upper bound.

change_log.change: Reframed the N = 21 experiment as a meaningful compiled demonstration with limited scope.
change_log.reason: Its quantum interference and recycling results should be preserved without treating one historical experiment as a survey of all later work.

change_log.change: Removed categorical assertions of worldwide nonachievement, historical priority and absence of journal publication.
change_log.reason: The supplied record lacks a comprehensive freshness survey and does not establish those present-day claims.

change_log.change: Strengthened completion proposals with independently selected unknown-answer instances, execution records and repeated demonstrations.
change_log.reason: Mathematical answer verification alone does not establish quantum provenance, reproducibility or breadth.

change_log.change: Integrated source-access limitations alongside the affected results.
change_log.reason: The cat-qubit extraction was incomplete, the Nature main article was a subscription preview, and the phase-flip correction came from the associated peer-review file.

change_log.change: Added distinctions covering all supplied roster entries, including QUA-08.
change_log.reason: Although the review lacked QUA-08’s description, the final inputs supply its title. Title-based synthesis is possible without inventing detailed requirements or relative timing.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the worldwide frontier of Shor experiments or hardware as of 1 November 2026, including whether a cryptographically relevant execution has occurred elsewhere.
Whether either retained arXiv work has a later journal publication is not established.
The detailed cat-qubit derivation in Appendix C9 and its experimental-state appendix were outside the retained extraction.
The extent to which either projected architecture can sustain all assumed noise, connectivity and timing properties simultaneously at full scale remains unestablished by the supplied experiments.
Detailed technical relationships and relative timing among the roster concepts, particularly QUA-08, cannot be determined from titles alone.

prerequisites.reason: Cryptographically relevant execution of Shor’s algorithm uses sustained, error-corrected logical operations to complete the cryptographic circuit.
